messages.subject: Averaging psi and SE(psi) over fixed-factor levels
messages.subject_clean: Averaging psi and SE(psi) over fixed-factor levels
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked community

I have a simulated detection/non-detection dataset with 1000 sites and 5 visits each with a habitat covariate of 5 factor levels as predictor for occupancy psi and no covariate for detection p:

fm <- occu(~1 ~habitat-1, data=umf)

My main interest is not in the habitat-specific estimates but in the averaged psi across the habitats. I would also like to get a corresponding standard error. For psi, I have taken the mean of the level-specific estimates on the logit-scale and then back-transformed the mean to probability scale:

mean.psi.prob <- plogis(mean(fm@opt$par[1:5]))

(Taking the mean over the level-specific estimates on the probability scale directly resulted in slightly different and possibly biased values)

I am now wondering how I can get a standard error of that mean.

1. Is it reasonable to average over the 5 level-specific standard errors on the logit-scale and interpret that as standard error of their mean?

I tried this approach but am uncertain of whether it is appropriate:

mean.se.logit <- mean(sqrt(diag(fm@estimates@estimates$state@covMat)[1:5]))

The follow-up question would be:

2. How do I then back-transform the averaged standard error to the probability scale?

I have tried the back-transformation via delta-method as it is described in the book “Bayesian Population Analysis Using WinBUGS” by Kéry & Schaub 2012 (p.185; they refer to Powell 2007):

mean.se.prob <- sqrt(mean.se.logit^2 * mean.psi.prob^2 * (1-mean.psi.prob)^2)

This back-transformation seems to give reasonable estimates, but if I apply it to the level-specific estimates directly and compare the output with the standard errors on the probability scale stored directly in the model output, they are similar but not identical:

se.prob1 <- unlist(predict(fm, "state",  newdata=data.frame(habitat=as.character(1:5))))[6:10]

psi.prob <- unlist(predict(fm, "state",  newdata=data.frame(habitat=as.character(1:5))))[1:5]

se.logit <- mean(sqrt(diag(fm@estimates@estimates$state@covMat)[1:5]))

se.prob2 <- sqrt(se.logit^2 * psi.prob^2 * (1-psi.prob)^2)

cbind(se.prob1, se.prob2)

      se.prob1   se.prob2

SE1 0.02326540 0.01827892

SE2 0.02909899 0.02936962

SE3 0.03208047 0.03550195

SE4 0.02609913 0.02422178

SE5 0.03224151 0.04268796

This leads me to the last question:

3. How are standard errors (which are presumably calculated on the logit scale in the model optimization) transformed to probability scale by the occu function in unmarked?

I could not find information on the link function used for standard error back-transformation in the package description.

Data are attached to this email and the full code is given below. Thank you in advance for any input!

Best wishes

Gesa

library(unmarked)

# load data objects

load("data.RData")

# create unmarked frame

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, siteCovs=data.frame(habitat=habitat))

# define initial values

int <- c(qlogis(runif(5)),    # occupancy parameters: 5 levels

         qlogis(runif(1)))    # detection parameter: intercept-only

# fit model

fm <- occu(~1 ~habitat-1, data=umf, starts=int, control=list(maxit=1000))

# compare output-delivered SE on probability scale to SEs calculated manually via delta-method

se.prob1 <- unlist(predict(fm, "state",  newdata=data.frame(habitat=as.character(1:5))))[6:10]

psi.prob <- unlist(predict(fm, "state",  newdata=data.frame(habitat=as.character(1:5))))[1:5]

se.logit <- mean(sqrt(diag(fm@estimates@estimates$state@covMat)[1:5]))

se.prob2 <- sqrt(se.logit^2 * psi.prob^2 * (1-psi.prob)^2)

cbind(se.prob1, se.prob2)

# these are NOT identical --> perhaps unmarked uses a different back-transformation?

# calculate mean psi across habitat levels

mean.psi.prob <- plogis(mean(fm@opt$par[1:5]))

# calculate SE of mean psi

mean.se.logit <- mean(sqrt(diag(fm@estimates@estimates$state@covMat)[1:5]))

mean.se.prob <- sqrt(mean.se.logit^2 * mean.psi.prob^2 * (1- mean.psi.prob)^2)

mean.psi.prob; mean.se.prob

# ... are these estimates reliable...?

messages.body_plain:
I'm going to take what some consider the standard statistician approach and not exactly answer your question.

Because there are 5 visits to each site and each habitat has on the average 200 sites, the detection probability is probably adequately estimated for each habitat analyzed separately.  For each of the 5 analyses the backTransform function is used to obtain an estimate of the mean occupancy and standard deviation.  Then one combines those into an overall mean and standard error:

# fit models
fm1 <- occu(~1 ~1, unmarkedFrameOccu(y=umf@y[umf@siteCovs$habitat==1,]))
fm2 <- occu(~1 ~1, unmarkedFrameOccu(y=umf@y[umf@siteCovs$habitat==2,]))
fm3 <- occu(~1 ~1, unmarkedFrameOccu(y=umf@y[umf@siteCovs$habitat==3,]))
fm4 <- occu(~1 ~1, unmarkedFrameOccu(y=umf@y[umf@siteCovs$habitat==4,]))
fm5 <- occu(~1 ~1, unmarkedFrameOccu(y=umf@y[umf@siteCovs$habitat==5,]))

# Backtransform
psi1 <- backTransform(fm1, 'state')
psi2 <- backTransform(fm2, 'state')
psi3 <- backTransform(fm3, 'state')
psi4 <- backTransform(fm4, 'state')
psi5 <- backTransform(fm5, 'state')

# Calculate summary statistics
psi.mean <- mean(c(psi1@estimate, psi2@estimate, psi3@estimate, psi4@estimate, psi5@estimate))
# [1] 0.5636228
psi.se <http://psi.se> <- sqrt(sum(c(psi1@covMat, psi2@covMat, psi3@covMat, psi4@covMat, psi5@covMat)))/5
# [1] 0.0128643

This isn’t the most efficient method in that 5 separate estimates of the detection probability need to be obtained when under the assumptions all share the same value.  But with large sample sizes it really doesn’t matter and it’s relatively simple to do.  Plus this approach is probably more robust in that in real life Mother Nature is not going to have exactly equal detection probabilities in each habitat.  If the sample sizes were smaller and maybe the occupancy and detection probabilities were small, then this approach might not be so hot.

All standard maximum likelihood estimators of occupancy parameters are biased in some amount.  Here the bias would need to be derived with respect to the parameter of interest which seems to be mean(psi1, psi2, psi3, psi4, psi5) rather than plogis(mean(logitpsi1, logitpsi2, logitpsi3, logitpsi4, logitpsi5)).  (In other words the mean of the occupancy probabilities rather than the anti-logit of the mean of the logits of the occupancy probabilities.)  In this case where there are no continuous covariates, there's really no need to use a logistic transformation to obtain maximum likelihood estimates.

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Because for your data the number of visits per site is constant within habitats and the particular model has no continuous covariates, the formulas for the hessian (using the Delta Method - or the Propagation of Error if you're a physicist) used to construct the estimated covariance matrix are straightforward.

# Run analysis
  fm <- occu(~1 ~ 0 + habitat, umf)

# Get summary statistics (for which n0 and m are sufficient statistics)
# Number of sites for each habitat
  n <- table(umf@siteCovs$habitat)
  #  1   2   3   4   5
  #190 192 191 199 228
# Number of visits per site per habitat
  v <- rep(dim(umf@y)[2], length(n))
  #[1] 5 5 5 5 5
# Number of sites with no detections per habitat
  n0 <- tapply(1-apply(umf@y, 1, max), umf@siteCovs$habitat,sum)
  #  1   2   3   4   5
  # 22 153 140  32  87
# Number of detections per habitat
  m <- tapply(apply(umf@y, 1, sum),umf@siteCovs$habitat,sum)
  # 1   2   3   4   5
  #600 147 180 583 495
# Number of habitats
  k <- length(n)  # Number of habitats
  # 5

# Maximum likelihood estimates of parameters
  p = plogis(fm@opt$par[k+1])    # maximum likelihood estimate of p
  psi = plogis(fm@opt$par[1:k])  # maximum likelihood estimates of psi for each habitat

# Construct minus the hessian
  h <- matrix(rep(0,(k+1)^2), nrow=k+1)
  diag(h)[1:k] <- (n-n0)/psi^2 + n0*(1-(1-p)^v)^2/(1-psi+psi*(1-p)^v)^2
  h[1:k, k+1] <- (1-p)^(v-2)*n0*v/(1-psi+psi*(1-p)^v)^2
  h[k+1, 1:k] <- h[1:k, k+1]
  h[k+1, k+1] <- sum(m/p^2 + (v*(n-n0)-m)/(1-p)^2 +
    ((1-p)^(v-2) * n0*v*psi*(-(v-1)*(1-psi)+psi*(1-p)^v))/(1-psi+psi*(1-p)^v)^2)

# Covariance matrix
  covmat <- solve(h)

# Summary
  psi.mean <- mean(psi)
  # [1] 0.5636086
  psi.mean.se <http://psi.mean.se> <- sqrt(sum(diag(covmat)[1:k]))/k
  # [1] 0.01286833

Jim

Good afternoon,

My detection history comprehends detection information over 13 sites and 25 sampling occasions.
I also have 6 occupancy variables (say they are X1, X2, ... , X6) and 2 detection variables. The two detection variables are Trap Effort (camera-trap nights) and Human Use of Site (number of H. sapiens captures).

I have gone through several tutorials to try to fit the two detection variables in the obsCovs argument of the unmarkedFrameOccu function, but I have come across with some errors such as:

Error in validObject(.Object) :
  invalid class “unmarkedFrame” object: obsCovData does not have M*obsNum rows.

                                            siteCovs = siteCovs, # dataframe with detection and occupancy variables

                    ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6,
                    data = unmarkedFrameOccuObject)

(Later, I will use dredge() on GlobalModel)
Sorry if this is a very basic question, just want to make sure I am not running my models in a wrong way.

Thanks!
Regards,
Luís

messages.body_plain:
Hello there!

I am trying to estimate mammal occupancy.
For one of the species I am covering, it turns out that I am not exactly getting an error report but, whilst the detection estimates look ok, the occupancy ones are looking rather odd (Estimate = 1; SE = 0.00251; 95% confidence intervals: LL = 0.008984463, UL = 1).

I suspect that things might have taken a wrong turn during the backtransformation step. The way I did it was based on the information provided by Ian Fiske and Richard Chandler in their package overview (2.3 in https://cran.r-project.org/.../unm.../vignettes/unmarked.pdf <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/unmarked.pdf?fbclid=IwAR2fv8vsi3ydun61GYajCXomg83gOryxgVwer3eakQUrtUtbc3xAn9xfl0g>), but I don't know if I misunderstood the authors here or made a mistake elsewhere. In the authors' example, their coefficient argument (when using the backTransform in the fm2 model) is c(1, 0, 0), as they want to estimate detection and, in fm2, detection is modelled by two covariates.
I thought that the same would be true if my top model had occupancy being modelled by two covariates. However, my occupancy estimates seem to be odd.

I wonder where the wrong turn was (?) especially because, in species where the top model has only one covariate, or none, modelling occupancy/detection, the estimates for occupancy/detection come out alright. I tried to attach a few tables and a script regarding this issue, but it is not working, so please find them here:

https://wetransfer.com/downloads/c60c15c2e18b481c3b00d8611194af9f20220112193700/e0ff96c8a6c61f27c80c7984a214a26a20220112193743/845c68?fbclid=IwAR0YMXZ0E59U7Wtmn0VSkNeF79rJmjW8FByWj_rshvcPDB38JT6G5qxIaWE

. Let me know if you can't download them and I will dm them to you.

Thank you in advance!
Luís
